Accepted replies and stale question suppression

html:
Run controls, observation and reply handoff

Run controls translate observed server state into explicit user actions. A control acknowledgement, a later native snapshot and a terminal trace event are separate pieces of evidence. The browser must retain that distinction while a Pause, Stop, Resume, continuation or reply is in flight.

native_controls.js owns the desktop toolbar, request-specific pending actions, fallback snapshot reads, attachment selection and long-running operation controls. task_lifecycle.js supplies shared desktop/mobile action projection, stable buttons, stop-summary preferences and accepted-reply fences. The surrounding shell owns task cards, conversation navigation, interaction forms and trace subscriptions.

For server execution and authority, see request lifecycle, checks and authority and conversation coordination. For instruction delivery and application, see instruction editor flows.

Ownership and data flow

flowchart TD Server[Native execution and task owners] --> Snapshot[Canonical conversation snapshot] Server --> Direct[Fallback native request reads] Snapshot --> Projection[Per-request native control projection] Direct --> Projection Pending[Local pending command identities] --> Projection Projection --> Actions[Shared lifecycle action map and stable controls] Projection --> Interaction[Public OAuth and interaction presentation] Projection --> Progress[Task board, context usage and foreground progress] Actions --> User[Explicit user action] User --> Command[Request-scoped command helper] Command --> Pending Command --> API[Native command endpoint] API --> Server API -->|acknowledgement| Pending Server --> Trace[Trace events and retained output] Trace --> Shell[Shell card and accepted-reply reconciliation] Snapshot --> Shell Shell --> Projection Capacity[Observed global capacity] --> Label[Advisory capacity label]

The native controller is page-lived. init merges shell hooks, mounts its toolbar and binds top-level Stop/Pause/visibility listeners once. It replaces its fallback update subscription when reinitialized. When a canonical conversation owner exists, that owner supplies the existing invalidation transport. There is no public controller disposal method and no task-state polling timer. The foreground elapsed-time timer only updates text.

Each task view is keyed by request ID. Disconnected views are removed from the controller map. A settled terminal presentation can determine task-action status, while inline instruction routing still uses native execution state; an older completed trace must not disguise a live input or approval wait.

The shared lifecycle owner prefers an explicit lifecycle.actions map. An empty map is still explicit authority, not a reason to enable legacy defaults. continue_next separately carries observed advancement authority. Older snapshots use bounded compatibility rules based on explicit capabilities and state. A continued parent exposes no actions. The server revalidates every command.

Snapshot reconciliation

sequenceDiagram participant I as Shared invalidation owner participant C as Canonical conversation reader participant N as Native controls participant A as Native read API participant V as Task views and shell alt Selected canonical conversation I->>C: Refresh selected conversation C-->>N: Coherent conversation snapshot N->>N: Adopt non-older per-request revisions N->>N: Project current run and observed lane capacity N->>V: Update controls, steering observation and relevant state hooks else Direct or legacy request without a selected canonical owner I->>N: Request fallback refresh N->>N: Capture lifecycle revision, request and conversation N->>A: Read native state and required mounted request snapshots A-->>N: Snapshot evidence N->>N: Reject obsolete scope, lifecycle or state revision N->>V: Project accepted current evidence Note over N,A: More refresh callers can request a trailing pass end

applyConversation updates mounted request snapshots only when their revision is not older, then projects the current run and lane capacity. Its caller owns the conversation-level freshness fence. If there is no current run, the main native and credential presentation is cleared; request-specific views keep their own evidence.

Fallback refresh coalesces callers and performs a trailing pass when another call arrives during its read. A direct request can use its native endpoint; a conversation without an identified request first reads its latest native state. A complete latest result is reused instead of hydrating the same run again. Additional mounted requests can read compact snapshots in parallel.

Before regular projection, the controller checks its lifecycle revision, request, conversation and any retained per-view state revision. Read failures return a failed freshness result, while missing-request 404s are treated as absence. A fallback snapshot with continued_by can read the accepted child and hand it to the shell after rechecking request/conversation identity. Applying a provided canonical snapshot does not independently chase that child.

The main snapshot reader skips hidden pages. Visibility restoration asks the shared update owner to reconcile. Capacity has its own read/error state and never establishes execution truth. Its counters are observed availability, not a promise that a particular queued task can start: dependencies, targets and server scheduling still govern admission.

Explicit commands and pending state

Action Request sent and ownership boundary
Pause / Resume Native control POST with action: pause or resume; optional command context and retry fields remain explicit.
Stop Native control POST with action: cancel and the selected save_summary value. Force stop sends mode: instant with summary disabled.
Confirmation denial Confirmation POST with action: deny and empty context; this is a separate branch of the Stop helper.
Completion retry Resume with retry_completion: true and the exact decision_id.
Task Contract retry Resume with retry_task_contract: true and the supplied or snapshot-advertised contract_attempt_id.
Continue / Restart POST the request's continue or restart endpoint, then hand the accepted attempt to the captured conversation owner.
Skip / Stop and advance POST continue-next with the observed next_task_id, version, action and applicable summary choice.
Compact context Native control POST with action: compact, then publish context usage and refresh compaction evidence.
Follow-up / Steering Use the explicit instruction endpoints and supplied retry/resource identity described in instruction editor flows.
sequenceDiagram participant U as User participant N as Native command helper participant A as Server command owner participant C as Canonical reconciliation participant V as Request-specific controls U->>N: Pause, Resume or Stop for one request N->>N: Check per-request pending transition before proceeding N->>V: Show pending state for that request N->>A: POST explicit command and supported options alt Command acknowledged A-->>N: Accepted state or stop metadata N->>N: Advance local Pause/Resume/Cancel read fence opt Accepted stop metadata is present N->>V: Project accepted stop without claiming termination end N->>C: Reconcile, with trailing invalidation after committed Stop C-->>V: Current authoritative snapshot else Command delivery fails A--xN: Rejection or uncertain transport outcome N->>V: Restore local action availability opt Stop outcome is unconfirmed N-->>U: Task may still be running, retry Stop end end

Pending sets are per request, so one card's action does not select another card's task. Pause refuses a duplicate or a request already stopping. Resume refuses a pending resume/advance. Other continuation helpers have their own transition gates; these are UI coordination, not replacements for server locking.

Pause clears its pending flag after failure; observed paused, stopped or terminal state also clears obsolete pause intent. Resume refreshes after either outcome, and failure advances the local read fence before that refresh. An acknowledged Pause, Resume or Cancel advances the fence; unrelated commands do not all share that exact mechanism.

Stop can immediately project returned stop metadata while waiting for subsequent native truth. It requests a trailing canonical invalidation so an already-running pre-Stop read cannot remain the last displayed state. An unfinished graceful Stop continues to offer Force stop. Its accepted response does not prove that every external effect or process has ended.

The Save summary choice defaults on, is cached per request and is persisted best-effort in sessionStorage. Mounted switches for the same request synchronize. Force stop disables summary saving. Summary text is derived from the supplied stop phase; the browser does not generate the summary.

Attempts and queue advancement

flowchart TD Action[Explicit task action] --> Kind{Which identity changes?} Kind -->|Resume or compiler retry| Existing[POST control for the same request] Existing --> Observe[Reconcile the same request] Kind -->|Continue or Restart| Attempt[POST continuation or restart endpoint] Attempt --> Accepted[Server returns accepted attempt identity] Accepted --> Shell[Captured conversation owner adopts or observes child] Kind -->|Skip or Stop and advance| Next[Read snapshot next-task ID and version] Next --> Advance[POST continue-next with exact observed target] Advance --> Server[Server decides advancement and execution eligibility] Server --> Refresh[Refresh queue and native evidence] Shell --> Refresh Observe --> Refresh

Continue and Restart capture the current conversation for their acceptance callback and suppress repeated clicks for the corresponding request transition. Restart does not undo actions from the earlier attempt. Skip carries action: skip; Stop and advance carries action: stop and the summary preference. Both use the server's observed next-task identity/version rather than selecting a browser row at execution time. Failure refreshes observed truth and restores pending controls.

Compaction is an explicit mutation. After its response, the shell can read trace evidence to update the displayed context history. It is not part of passive snapshot refresh. The authoritative context behavior is described in Context.

Attachment selection and asynchronous boundaries

sequenceDiagram participant U as User or resource palette participant N as Attachment owner participant A as Context API participant D as Next-request draft U->>N: Choose files or a retained Context/artifact N->>N: Check steering lock, scope revision and remaining slots alt Upload files loop Selected files in order N->>N: Check 64 MiB file limit and current scope N->>A: Upload file bytes A-->>N: Public Context metadata N->>N: Recheck revision, scope, lock and capacity N->>D: Adopt eligible metadata end else Link an existing source N->>A: Link source into captured target conversation A-->>N: Public Context metadata N->>N: Recheck target, revision, scope and lock N->>D: Adopt a new eligible Context identity end Note over N,A: Ignoring a late response does not undo accepted server storage or grants

Local selection is bounded to 16 Context sources. Sanitization takes the first 16 supplied entries, rejects malformed or duplicate Context IDs and copies bounded names/media types and valid nonnegative sizes. It is a presentation/draft snapshot, not an authority grant.

Changing attachment scope, restoring a draft or changing steering lock advances the local attachment revision. The file picker captures that revision before the operating-system dialog opens. Uploads run serially and check both sides of each await; earlier accepted files remain if a later upload fails. File selection is cleared after the handler finishes. Linking requires an existing target conversation and rechecks it after the response.

Removing a chip removes it from the next request only; it does not delete the underlying source or revoke a server grant. During steering, this toolbar locks attachment changes. Inline instruction editors have their separate resource owner. Context-read labels are advisory, loaded independently with a newest-render fence; their failure does not discard attachment metadata. See composer resource flows for server link/grant boundaries and discovery.

Foreground operation decisions

sequenceDiagram participant S as Native snapshot owner participant N as Foreground panel participant U as User participant A as Operation control API S-->>N: Long-running operation identity and configured ceiling N->>N: Render elapsed time once per second without network reads U->>N: Keep Running or Terminate N->>A: POST captured request and operation ID with decision A-->>N: Acknowledged operation decision N->>N: Retain local decision overlay while snapshots catch up N->>S: Request normal reconciliation S-->>N: Updated operation or terminal/cancelled state N->>N: Update choices or remove panel and elapsed timer

The panel appears only for a long-running foreground operation on a nonterminal, non-cancelling request. Silence sends no command and does not pause execution. Keep Running and Terminate bind to the captured request/operation identity, rather than whichever run later becomes selected. The server owns the runtime ceiling and the actual operation outcome. A failed decision restores its button and displays an error.

Accepted replies and stale question suppression

sequenceDiagram participant A as Interaction acknowledgement participant L as Shared reply fence participant S as Snapshot or trace stream participant V as Existing task card A->>L: Same request, answered question and stream cursor L->>L: Capture question identity, trace epoch and maximum observed cursor S-->>L: Replayed old wait or older event L->>V: Suppress the answered form without claiming progress alt New nonpending execution or terminal evidence S-->>L: Current progress state or recognized event L->>L: Mark receipt no longer pending L->>V: Permit current state presentation else A new question is published S-->>L: New operation identity or supported legacy question evidence L->>L: Release answered wait and retain next-question evidence L->>V: Allow the new question else Trace epoch changes S-->>L: Different execution epoch L->>L: Mark old receipt obsolete end

replyAccepted records the greater of the caller's observed cursor and the acknowledgement stream's after_id. observeReply uses request, epoch, cursor, question identity and recognized state transitions to decide whether an older wait must stay suppressed. Its boolean is not a general “execution resumed” signal: unrelated evidence can return false without establishing progress. Pending state is tracked separately.

A later question can release the fence through a new operation identity or the supported legacy publication evidence. After progress, the retained identity still rejects replay of the answered wait. Reload restoration requires both the reply handoff shape and reset native_outcome: running metrics; an unpublished first question is insufficient. The shell reuses request-owned DOM and cursor state when an acknowledgement arrives after a snapshot already mounted the task.

Public interaction and data controls

The native controller forwards an OAuth descriptor only when the current state is waiting_user, its kind is oauth and its request ID matches. The API projection uses public HTTP-session fields: authorization URL, verification URI, user code and device marker. Public URLs can therefore appear in this UI state; private session credentials are not projected by that helper.

The toolbar also delegates task-permission editing to the shell. Export reads the conversation archive, downloads its response Blob and revokes the temporary browser URL. Retention uses explicit user confirmation before sending the selected action to the native-conversation API; artifact-policy selection opens the artifact owner instead. These handlers report the server result. They do not implement retention or infer that active work was cancelled. See conversation lifecycle and artifacts for the corresponding state owners.

Evidence and scope

Both browser modules were reviewed in full. Shell integration and the public OAuth projection were reviewed at their stated boundaries. Focused evidence includes lifecycle controls, summary preferences, reply ordering, pause presentation and foreground decisions. Selected cases use Node or isolated Chromium with fake services/intercepted APIs. The review ledger retains pass results and baseline failures separately; these checks do not certify live external-process termination or physical mobile devices.
